# Workshop Bench Build

## Overview

The bench is the first piece of furniture I built for the workshop and it is still the most used. It runs along the end wall, 2.4 m long and 900 mm high, with a top I can hammer on without it drumming. The design is deliberately dull: a laminated top on a frame of thick timber, with the whole thing heavy enough that it does not walk across the floor when I plane a board on it. I sketched it on the back of an envelope, then drew the final version properly because the vice needed a mounting block in exactly the right place. It took two weekends, most of which was waiting for glue to dry, and it has outlasted three projects that needed a better bench than I had before. It is not pretty. The edges are rounded because I rounded them, and the top has picked up a few stains that I have no intention of sanding out. What matters is that it is dead flat, dead quiet, and heavy enough to stay put, and those three things are the whole reason it took two weekends to build rather than one. A bench is the one piece of workshop furniture that everything else depends on, so it is the one piece I built to last rather than to look at.

## Building

I built the top first, because the frame dimensions follow from it. The top is two 18 mm MDF skins over a 100 mm egg-crate core, which is a grid of thin ribs between the two skins. The core does the work: it makes the top stiff and quiet without making it heavy, and it saves a great deal of material compared with one solid slab. I cut the ribs, laid the grid out on the lower skin, glued and pinned them down, and then glued the upper skin on and piled everything I could find on top for weight while it cured.

When the top came out of the clamps I gave the edges a strip of solid timber so a bump would not chip the MDF, and I routed the edges round so my forearms are not resting on a corner all day. Then I built the frame. The legs are thick and the aprons tie them together at the top, just under the top, which is where the stiffness comes from. The aprons are bolted rather than screwed into the legs so the bench can be taken apart if it ever has to move.

The vice goes on the left end. I put it on the left because I am right-handed and that gives me room to work along the bench towards the middle. Under the vice I bolted a mounting block between two aprons, so the force of a heavy cut goes into the frame rather than into the top alone. I checked the jaws were square to the front edge before I tightened anything up, because a vice out of square is worse than no vice.

Then the dog holes. I bored them at 150 mm centres along the front of the top, in a line, so a bench dog and the vice can hold a long board between them. I drilled the first hole, dropped a dog in, and used that to keep the line straight as I moved along, which is faster than marking 150 mm repeatedly and less prone to drift. At the end I checked the line with a straightedge across the whole length.

The height is 900 mm, which suits me standing. I set the frame up and tried a few hand-plane passes at that height before I committed to it, because a bench at the wrong height is a bench I would not use. Once the height was right I glued and bolted everything together, checked it was level and did not rock, and then finished the top with oil and wax. The oil goes on first, a few coats with a cloth, and the wax goes over the top to give a surface that is smooth to the hand and easy to refresh.

## Notes

The bench is heavier than it looks and moving it is a two-person job, which is the only design regret I have. The saving is that it never moves on its own. The egg-crate core is worth the extra hour of cutting, because the top is dead under a mallet and my chisels thank me. Oil and wax is the right finish for a work surface, since it is easy to patch and does not crack like a film finish does when it is hit. If I built it again I would add a second row of dog holes further back, and I would drill the holes before I put the top on the frame so I could use the drill press. As it is, the bench does everything I ask of it and I have stopped thinking about replacing it. The one addition I would make is a shelf underneath, because the space under the bench is where the offcuts go to hide, and a shelf would turn that pile into a place I can reach. The height of 900 mm is worth checking against your own elbows before you cut anything, since a bench a centimetre wrong is a bench you notice every single day, and no amount of good joinery makes up for the wrong height.
